evidence: Catull. 46.6: ad clārās Asiae volēmus urbēs
terms.comment: First bright and clear, of light, and loud, of sound (see loud); then clear to the mind, and famous, with the ablative of what for. The superlative clārissimus was the standing title of senators and consuls (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: well known, famous; of noble birth
evidence: Phaedr. App. 21.1: equum … multīs palmīs nōbilem
terms.comment: From nōscō: known, and so famous, often with the ablative of what for (Traupman 204: famous for). Of people it usually means noble, of a family that has held high office (Lewis & Short).

First crowded, much visited (locus celeber, a busy place); “famous” mostly from Augustan writers on (Lewis & Short). The verb celebrāre is to throng, and so to make famous: Tagus auriferīs harēnīs celebrātur (Plin. NH 4.115).
Very fine, noble, remarkable; famous as a work of praise rather than of report.

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Enn., Lucr., Verg., Hor.; not in Caesar or Cicero (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: let’s fly to the famous cities of Asia

phrases.latin: oppida ā Tagō memorābilia in ōrā Olisīpō, equārum ē favōniō ventō conceptū nōbile
phrases.english: the notable towns on the coast from the Tagus: Lisbon, famous for its mares conceived by the west wind

phrases.latin: etiam dicta clārōrum virōrum et ēlēctōs ex poētīs maximē … locōs ēdiscere inter lūsum licet
phrases.english: even the sayings of famous men and passages chosen mostly from the poets can be learned by heart in play
